title: Oriental Fruit Fly: How to Spot It and Protect Your Mango and Papaya
metaTitle: Oriental Fruit Fly: Signs, Damage and Control
metaDescription: The oriental fruit fly lays eggs in mango, papaya and guava, and the maggots rot the fruit from inside. Learn the signs and how to control it step by step.
excerpt: The oriental fruit fly is a small fly whose maggots rot mango, papaya, guava and many other fruits from the inside. The fruit looks fine at first, then it drops or turns soft. This page shows how to spot the oriental fruit fly and how to keep it out of your harvest.

heroImage.alt: An oriental fruit fly, Bactrocera dorsalis, yellow and dark brown, on a green leaf

blocks.text:
The oriental fruit fly (Bactrocera dorsalis) is native to Asia and is also called the papaya fruit fly. The Pacific Pests sheet calls it highly destructive, and UF reports that it attacks 478 kinds of fruits and vegetables, with avocado, mango and papaya most at risk. It also hits banana, citrus, capsicum, grapes and tomato, and wild plants such as Ficus and Terminalia.

The female also puts bacteria into the fruit when she lays eggs, and these bacteria rot the flesh. The fruit then drops early. A single female may lay 1,200 to 1,500 eggs in the field, according to UF. That is why a few flies can ruin a whole harvest. See also the [melon fly](/pests/melon-fly), a close relative that attacks gourds.

blocks.caption: Quick facts
rows: Mango, papaya, guava, avocado, banana, citrus and some vegetables such as tomato and pepper
It attacks as the fruit nears ripening, and most flies arrive during the fruiting season of mango, guava and papaya.

The female pierces ripe or ripening fruit and lays eggs inside. The eggs hatch in about a day, and the maggots feed for about 2 weeks. Then they drop to the soil to pupate. Egg to adult takes about 16 days in good conditions.

blocks.text: How to Identify Oriental Fruit Fly

Look for small egg laying marks, called stings, on the fruit skin. Cut a fruit that has begun to soften and you will find creamy white maggots, about 10 mm when full grown. The adult fly is about 7 mm long. It has a black thorax with two yellow stripes, a brown to yellow abdomen with a T shaped mark, and clear wings with a brown band along the front edge. The [mango cecid fly](/pests/mango-cecid-fly) and the [mango pulp weevil](/pests/mango-pulp-weevil) damage mango too, so check what you find inside the fruit.

items: Small sting marks on the fruit skin where the female laid eggs.
Fruit that softens, rots or drops before it is ripe.
Creamy white maggots inside the flesh.
Fruit that ripens too early or goes soft where the eggs were laid.
Many flies on fallen fruit under the tree.
Fruit that looks sound at first but rots from the inside within days.

blocks.title: Do not confuse it with
blocks.text: The [melon fly](/pests/melon-fly) is similar, but it stings gourds such as ampalaya and upo. Several other fruit flies also look alike, so for a sure name, bring a few flies to your agricultural technician.
How Oriental Fruit Fly Hurts Your Crop

The Pacific Pests sheet describes premature fruit drop within days of egg laying, and heavy yield losses in mango and guava in Thailand. When the fly entered Australia in 1995, it took 4 years and 33 million dollars to wipe it out. The fly can also close export markets, because its presence can limit export opportunities.

We found no Philippine action threshold in the sources we read. The usual rule is to trap and watch from the time the fruit is half grown, and to act as soon as the traps catch flies.
How to Control Oriental Fruit Fly

items: Hang traps with methyl eugenol in the shade of the trees to watch the males. The lure only monitors and draws the males, so it does not protect the fruit by itself.
Pick up and destroy every fallen and overripe fruit each few days. Bury it deep or seal it in a plastic bag in the sun, so the maggots cannot pupate in the soil.
Bag the fruit at least 6 weeks before harvest, as the Pacific Pests sheet suggests, so the females cannot reach it.
Harvest at the mature green stage when your buyer allows it. The flies prefer ripe fruit.
Prune the canopy to improve air flow, and keep wild host plants such as guava and Ficus away from the orchard edge.
Work with your neighbors, because the flies travel from tree to tree. See the [integrated pest management guide](/pests/integrated-pest-management).

blocks.text: Pacific Pests prefers protein bait sprays to broad cover sprays. The bait draws the flies, and the insecticide in it kills them. Apply it 5 to 8 weeks before harvest to a few spots of the canopy, not to the fruit. Follow the FPA registered label and the waiting time. Older sprays such as malathion and pyrethroids caused resistance and harmed the environment.

blocks.caption: Active ingredients that work. Always follow the label of an FPA registered product.

blocks.title: Spray safely
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label for the rate, the timing and the protective clothing. Switch to a different insecticide group next time, so the pest does not learn to survive it. Our [guide to integrated pest management](/pests/integrated-pest-management) explains how.

items: Keep the orchard floor clean of fallen fruit all through the season.
Bag the fruit well before harvest.
Use traps from half grown fruit on, so you act before the fly builds up.
Plan your planting and harvest dates with neighbors to break the fly's food supply.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Oriental Fruit Fly

items.q: Why do my mangoes rot from inside even though the skin looks fine?
items.a: The oriental fruit fly may have laid eggs under the skin. The maggots rot the flesh while the skin still looks fine. Cut a soft fruit open and look for maggots.

items.q: Does a methyl eugenol trap protect my fruit?
items.a: Not by itself. It draws and catches the males and tells you when flies are around. Bagging, removing fallen fruit and bait sprays protect the fruit.

items.q: When should I put out the bait spray?
items.a: Pacific Pests says 5 to 8 weeks before harvest. Mix the protein bait with the insecticide and spray it on part of the canopy.
